quote: Indeed, it seems there is no way to justify Occam’s Razor except by appealing to Occam’s Razor, making this argument unlikely to convince any judge who does not already accept Occam’s Razor.
content: There is a non-circular partial justification, and it is in the literature the essay is summarizing. Kelly’s Ockham efficiency theorems (Kelly (2007)) show that a learner who always adopts the simplest hypothesis consistent with the data minimizes the number of retractions, the times it must reverse itself, before converging on the truth, and that this holds whatever the truth turns out to be, simple or complex. That is a justification of the razor as the most efficient route to the truth rather than as an assumption that the world is simple, and it does not appeal to the razor. Whether it is enough is debated, but its existence dissolves the essay’s dilemma between circularity and “a priori.” The essay’s own answer, “we live in a simple world, a low-entropy universe in which there are short explanations to be found,” is the circular one: the evidence that the world is simple was gathered with the razor, and the essay’s admission that it does not know why the universe is orderly is the admission that the justification stops there. The philosophers who use “a priori” as a white flag were, on this point, being more careful than the essay allows, and the no-free-lunch theorems (Wolpert (1996)) say why: no inductive bias is justified by data alone.

quote: When “pure thought” tells you that 1 + 1 = 2, “independently of any experience or observation,” you are, in effect, observing your own brain as evidence.
content: This is psychologism, and Frege’s objection to it (Grundlagen der Arithmetik, 1884, Introduction and §§26–27) has not been answered by anyone, including this essay. If “1 + 1 = 2” were a report of what brains do when they collide the patterns for 1 and 1, then it would be a contingent generalization about brains, refutable by a brain that outputs 3, and it would have been false before there were brains. It is none of these. Brains that compute 1 + 1 = 3 are wrong, and their wrongness is not a fact about a statistical majority of other brains; it is a fact about arithmetic. The essay confuses the causal question (how does a brain come to believe the proposition?) with the justificatory one (what makes the proposition true and the belief warranted?), which is the genetic fallacy, and the confusion becomes acute later in the same book: Beautiful Probability calls the laws of probability “theorems” and “laws” that hold whether or not any brain obeys them, which is exactly the status this essay denies to arithmetic. If a priori knowledge is observation of one’s own neural engine, the theorems of probability are observations of the engine too, and the book’s repeated claim that they are “harder than steel” is a claim about the reader’s neurons.

quote: Are the sort of neural flashes that philosophers label “a priori beliefs” arbitrary? Many AI algorithms function better with “regularization” that biases the solution space toward simpler solutions. But the regularized algorithms are themselves more complex; they contain an extra line of code (or 1,000 extra lines) compared to unregularized algorithms. The human brain is biased toward simplicity, and we think more efficiently thereby.
content: The human simplicity bias has been measured, and it is not the well-calibrated efficiency the essay describes. People prefer the simpler of two candidate explanations even when the more complex one is more probable on the stated evidence, and they require a large probability advantage before they abandon the simpler one (Lombrozo (2007)); the bias is real and it is a bias, in the sense this book uses the word. The regularization analogy also proves less than it appears to: regularization improves generalization when the regularizer matches the structure of the problem, and the wrong regularizer degrades it, which is the no-free-lunch point again. So the brain’s preference for simplicity is neither arbitrary nor a truth factory; it is an inductive bias that pays off in environments of a certain kind and misfires in others, and the interesting empirical question, which environments, is the one the essay’s engine metaphor does not ask.

quote: If a mind doesn’t implement Modus Ponens, it can accept “A” and “A → B” all day long without ever producing “B.” How do you justify Modus Ponens to a mind that hasn’t accepted it? How do you argue a rock into becoming a mind?
content: This is Lewis Carroll’s “What the Tortoise Said to Achilles” (Carroll (1895)), in which the Tortoise accepts A and A → B and every further conditional Achilles supplies, and never accepts B; the regress it exhibits, that a rule of inference cannot be one of the premises it is applied to, is one of the most discussed short papers in philosophy, and the essay presents its content as an original observation about engines. The conclusion the essay draws, that some rules must be implemented rather than justified, is the standard one (Ryle’s knowing-how, Quine’s “Truth by Convention,” 1936; Boghossian, “Blind Reasoning” (Proceedings of the Aristotelian Society, Supplementary Volume, 2003) on rule-circular justification). The essay is entitled to the conclusion; it is not entitled to present the philosophers who reached it first as people waving a white flag, since the white flag, on inspection, is a hundred-year-old argument that they were right to wave it.
